  a legend.

  Legendary Origins in China

  According to Chinese tradition, tea was discovered in 2737 BCE by Shennong, the mythical "Divine
  Farmer" credited with teaching agriculture and herbal medicine to the Chinese people. In the
  story, Shennong was boiling drinking water beneath a wild tea tree when a few leaves drifted into
  his pot. He tasted the faintly bitter, fragrant result and found it refreshing and restorative.
  The tale is almost certainly apocryphal, but it captures something true. In China, tea was first
  valued as medicine, a tonic believed to clear the mind and sharpen the senses.

  The archaeological record is more modest but still impressive. The oldest physical tea leaves yet
  identified were found in the mausoleum of Emperor Jing of Han, who died in 141 BCE. They were
  buried alongside him as a luxury fit for the afterlife. Written references from the same era show
  that tea was being bought and sold in the markets of Sichuan. The tea plant itself probably
  originated in the borderlands where southwestern China meets Myanmar and northeastern India. Wild
  tea trees there still grow to towering heights, and local peoples chewed or pickled the leaves
  long before anyone thought to steep them.

  The Tang and Song Dynasties: Tea Becomes Culture

  Tea moved from medicine to everyday pleasure during the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE), a period of
  prosperity and cosmopolitan confidence. Its defining document appeared around 760 CE, when the
  scholar Lu Yu wrote the Cha Jing, or Classic of Tea. It was the first known book devoted entirely
  to the subject. Lu Yu described how tea was cultivated, how it should be processed, which waters
  were best for brewing, and what implements a refined drinker should own. In his time, tea leaves
  were steamed, pounded and pressed into cakes. Pieces of the cake were roasted, ground and boiled,
  sometimes with salt. Lu Yu turned tea drinking into an art with an aesthetic and moral dimension,
  and he was later revered as the "Sage of Tea."

  Under the Song dynasty (960–1279), fashion changed again. Tea was now ground into a fine powder
  and whisked with hot water in a bowl until it formed a pale froth. Whisked-tea competitions became
  popular among the elite, and the emperor Huizong wrote a treatise of his own on the subject.
  Dark-glazed ceramic bowls, prized because they showed off the white foam, became highly
  collectible. Tea was also a currency of state. The government ran a monopoly and traded tea for
  warhorses with Tibetan and Central Asian peoples along routes later called the Tea Horse Road,
  which wound through the mountains of Yunnan and Sichuan.

  The Ming Revolution: Loose Leaf

  The next transformation came under the Ming dynasty. In 1391, the Hongwu Emperor decreed that
  tribute tea should be presented as loose leaves rather than labor-intensive compressed cakes. The
  decision was partly practical and partly a gesture toward the common people. It reshaped how tea
  was made and consumed. Steeping whole leaves in a pot became standard, and new processing
